Group III, Indicator 2: Patients Developing New Disabilities Following Registration This indicator involves assessing all cases currently under treatment and those released from treatment within the last two years. Patients are visited, examined, and interviewed, and information is collected from recorded data and interviews. It is defined as the proportion of cases that develop new disabilities either during or after release from treatment (RFT). For example, a patient with no disability at the start of treatment (Grade 0) who develops anesthesia or paralysis in the hand during or after treatment is considered to have a new disability. Prerequisites include reviewing treatment registers and individual records. Monitors must collect information on: The clinical status, including disability assessments, of all cases released from treatment in the last two years and those currently under treatment. The total number of cases visited, which serves as the denominator. Example: In Nepal, as of October 2011, 20 cases had been released from treatment since October 2009. Of these, 15 were visited by the monitor. Additionally, five cases were under treatment, and all were visited. One patient was found to have developed a new disability, verified through patient statements and records. The proportion of new disabilities was 1 out of 20 (5%). Interpretation: This indicator is valuable for evaluating the quality of care. However, it is essential to consider the procedures used to follow up with patients and the completeness of records regarding disability. Group III, Indicator 3: Information is collected from registers and interviews, using a sample questionnaire provided in Annexure-1. The purpose is to assess patient satisfaction and identify areas for improvement in service quality. Definition: The proportion of cases that develop new disabilities during or after RFT. For example, a patient with no disability at the start of treatment who develops anesthesia or paralysis during or after treatment is considered to have a new disability. Prerequisites: Reviewing treatment registers and individual records. Monitors must collect information on: New cases registered in the last year. Contacting and interviewing these cases using a questionnaire. The total number of cases visited, which serves as the denominator. Stratifying new cases into adults and children, with 50% of adults randomly selected for interviews. Interpretation: This indicator is highly useful for evaluating care quality from the perspective of affected individuals. However, it is important to recognize that perceptions of quality depend on personal experiences and expectations. Careful interpretation of results is necessary. Group III, Indicator 4: It indirectly reflects the quality of services. Definition: The proportion of community members aware of the disease and the program. Calculation: At least five individuals from each village visited are selected and interviewed individually, not in groups. Interpretation: This indicator is valuable for assessing awareness levels and indirectly evaluating the quality of care from the perspective of end-users. However, various biases must be considered, and results should be interpreted cautiously. Group III, Indicator 5: Definition: The proportion of affected individuals reporting discrimination as perceived by them. Calculation: Interviews are conducted with all individuals released from treatment in the last two years, using a sample questionnaire provided in the annexure, with suitable modifications if needed. Interpretation: This indicator is highly useful for assessing the prevalence of negative attitudes within the community. Further Reading: 1. WHO's Enhanced Global Strategy for Further Reducing the Disease Burden Due to Leprosy (2011-2015) emphasizes early detection and quality care in integrated service settings. 2. Operational guidelines for the Enhanced Global Strategy (2011-2015) by WHO. 3. Leprosy Elimination Monitoring (LEM) guidelines by WHO, 2000. 4. Research articles on patient satisfaction and stigma, such as those by Salisbury et al. (2005) and Goffman (1963). 5. Guidelines to reduce stigma, published by the International Federation of Anti-Leprosy Associations (ILEP) and Netherlands Leprosy Relief (NLR), 2011. The Enhanced Global Leprosy Strategy (2011-2015) aims to reduce new cases with Grade-2 disabilities by 35% by the end of the strategy period. It highlights the importance of early detection and quality care in an integrated service setting. Monitoring and evaluation are essential components of leprosy control programs, using a minimum set of indicators to assess impact, effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, and sustainability. These indicators enable before-and-after analyses to evaluate program interventions. While routine data collection provides adequate information on progress and performance, it may not fully assess quality-of-care indicators.
